newsitem.title: USA: Dow edges lower on last day of powerhouse quarter.
newsitem.headline: Dow edges lower on last day of powerhouse quarter.

text.p: U.S. blue chips edged to narrow losses on Monday in a choppy conclusion to the stock market's strongest quarter in more than a decade.
The Dow dipped 15 points to close unofficially at 7673. Financial stocks were weaker, dragged lower by a soft bond market, while technology stocks were generally firm.
The session represented an understated conclusion to a second quarter in which the Dow surged nearly 1,100 points or 16.7 percent, its largest such gain since March 1987, when it soared 21.6 percent.

Stocks steered a see-saw course, stumbling early after stronger-than-expected data on U.S. new home sales and regional manufacturing activity. The figures sent the bond market reeling and dragged stocks to sharp early losses.

"The data obviously made people wonder if the economy is picking up steam again, and that got the whole question of interest rates surfacing again," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
Interest rate concerns are particularly acute issue this week because of the Federal Reserve's regularly scheduled two-day interest rate policy meeting, which begins Tuesday.

Most economists expect the Fed will leave interest rates unchanged at the meeting, but even so, market activity is likely to be subdued until Wednesday, when the central bank announces the result of the meeting.
Whatever the outcome, a number of analysts were casting a much more cautious eye to the market, given its remarkable performance in recent months.

Morgan Stanley Dean Witter strategist Barton Biggs raised cash in the firm's Balanced Financial Asset Portfolio to 15 percent from 10 percent, drawing down stocks to 53 percent from 58 percent, citing in part the recent exuberance.

"History shows that the most effective way to trade in and out of this sort of market is to go against extremes of sentiment," Biggs said in a note explaining the move. "All of this could be setting us up for something significant to happen this summer."
Analysts are often quick to point out that the fastest-won market gains are also often the quickest to be lost.

The ferocious gains of early 1987, for example, were followed by a 25.3 percent freefall in the fourth quarter, with most of that coming during the 508-point, 22.6 percent "Black Monday" plunge on October 19, 1987.

While few on Wall Street expect another market crash on the horizon, many caution that some backtracking is inevitable, especially if the bond market's worries over the strength of the economy and inflation continue to mount.

"A 10 percent pullback at this point would be my guess," said Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest. "We've had this lovely lull in the economy, and that's producing some strength in the market that's probably unsustainable."
Among individual issues, Rykoff-Sexton Inc jumped 3-11/16 to 23-5/16 after announcing a $1.4 billion stock swap merger with JP Foodservice Inc.
Shares in JP Foodservice, which will issue 0.84 of a share for each Rykoff share and assume $700 million in debt under terms of the deal, fell 1-7/16 to 28-11/16.
NationsBank Corp fell 11/16 to 64-9/16 after announcing it would acquire privately held investment bank Montgomery Securities for $1.2 billion in cash and stock.

Stratasys Inc tumbled 5-5/8 to 16-1/8 after the company warned its second-quarter revenues would fall short of estimates. The company, which makes rapid prototyping systems for the aerospace, automotive and other industries, linked the expected shortfall to production constraints.
The S&P 500 fell 2.16 to 885.14.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 3.92 to 1442.07.
